speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In today’s technology- and knowledge-driven economy, where intangible assets are increasingly important, a robust and trusted IP regime is essential for growth and enterprise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore is well-recognised internationally for its world-class IP regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the latest 2018 Global Competitiveness Report published by the World Economic Forum, Singapore is ranked third in the world, and first in Asia, for IP protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In today’s rapidly changing world, we cannot rest on our laurels and must continually assess and review our IP regime to ensure that it remains relevant and supports our enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill is very much in this vein.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Innovative and creative enterprises that develop IP and protect it can secure a commercial advantage over their competitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They can protect their IP in Singapore swiftly and efficiently through the suite of e-services that the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) provides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, they can also secure protection overseas with ease and speed through the international agreements and networks that Singapore is a part of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, international trademark registrations can be secured under the Madrid system, and international patent applications can be filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Patent applications in many major markets can also be accelerated under the Global Patent Prosecution Highway programme and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Patent Examination Cooperation programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, obtaining IP protection would have no commercial value to an enterprise if, when its IP rights are infringed, it finds itself unable to enforce its IP rights due to a lack of financial resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The cost-effective resolution of IP disputes increases the confidence that IP rights owners have in maintaining their competitive edge and maximising the rewards of their innovative and creative efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is an increase of almost 22% from five years earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The number of applications from locals has increased by even more, at about 40% from 2013 to 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The pace of innovation, by both local businesses and individuals, is accelerating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, therefore, not only must the IP registration process be cost-effective and easy to navigate, in the event that IP rights need to be enforced, the IP dispute resolution process must also be cost-effective and easy to navigate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was why in 2015, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) appointed a committee to review the IP dispute resolution system in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One of the objectives of the review was to make the IP dispute resolution system more accessible, particularly for less well-resourced parties, such as individuals and small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill implements some of the Committee’s recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are doing so from a position of strength.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An important plank of our legal and judicial system is the efficiency of our Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, this Bill strengthens Singapore’s position as a choice venue for the arbitration of international IP disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, we are legislating certain patent-related procedures before the Registrar of Patents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, we are clarifying that IP disputes may be arbitrated in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The first two groups of amendments facilitate the effective resolution of IP disputes in Court and at IPOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: IPOS is responsible for the Registries of the various IP rights, for example, the Registry of Patents and the Registry of Trade Marks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will first discuss dispute resolution in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill consolidates most civil IP disputes in a single forum – the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, IP disputes are heard in multiple forums, namely, the High Court, the State Courts and at IPOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where a dispute is to be heard depends on a few factors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, on the IP right in issue, for example, whether the dispute is about a patent over an invention, or copyright in song lyrics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, the nature of the dispute, for example, whether the dispute is about infringement of someone's IP right, or the validity of the IP right itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, a copyright or trade secret owner commences his case in the State Courts, if he or she is seeking damages of up to $250,000 for copyright infringement or breach of confidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Above this amount, the case must be commenced in the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On the other hand, for infringement of patents, trademarks and registered designs, the case must be started in the High Court, regardless of the value of the claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This, itself, adds complexity and different layers to determine which kinds of cases are commenced and heard in which Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Going forward, the IP dispute resolution system will be improved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the system will be streamlined, and it will be clearer to users what the appropriate forum is when they have a dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, parties who litigate in Court will benefit from the expertise of High Court judges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The High Court has a specialist bench of IP judges, with greater expertise and experience in IP matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, IP rights owners and users in general will benefit from the development of IP jurisprudence through High Court judgments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill, therefore, makes the following amendments to the jurisdiction of the Registrar of Patents, the Magistrate's Court, the District Court and the High Court over IP disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Cases before the Copyright Tribunal, for example, cases about licensing rates charged by copyright owners, are not affected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 13 and 19 remove the jurisdiction of the Registrar of Patents over patent infringement and declarations of non-infringement of patents, respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 20(a) gives the High Court jurisdiction over patent revocation, where such proceedings do not arise in the context of an existing dispute before the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 31 and 32 remove the jurisdiction of the Magistrate's Court and the District Court over an action in passing off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The High Court will also have concurrent jurisdiction with the relevant Registrar over post-grant revocation and invalidation proceedings for patents, and not just trademarks, registered designs and geographical indications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such proceedings are about whether the IP rights are validly registered or granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This gives the parties commencing revocation or invalidation proceedings a choice between doing so in the High Court and doing so before the relevant Registrar who granted the right in the first place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is outside the scope of this Bill and will be done via amendments to civil procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This "specialised track" will be especially useful for less well-resourced parties, such as individuals and SMEs, who may otherwise be unable to enforce their valid IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Litigants in the High Court will generally be able to choose between this "specialised track" for IP cases, and the "default track" where IP cases are treated in a similar manner to other types of civil cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: More details about the time and cost-saving features of the "specialised track" will be shared in due course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: My Ministry consulted practitioners when developing these reforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We received feedback that IP litigation tends to be more expensive than most other types of litigation, given its specialised and highly technical nature and, in some cases, the need for expert witnesses as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This could put it out of reach for some enterprises that need to turn to the Courts to resolve their disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This "specialised track" is being developed with a focus on lowering litigation costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, I turn to proceedings at IPOS, specifically those before the Registrar of Patents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill seeks to raise the quality of granted patents in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Before elaborating on the amendments, let me provide an overview of the patent application process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After a patent application is made at the Registry of Patents, it undergoes Search and Examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A patent examiner will search publicly available information at the time of the patent application to understand the current state of technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The examiner then assesses whether the invention in the application meets the statutory criteria of being new, inventive and capable of industrial application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Only inventions that fully meet these criteria are granted patent protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a process in which a third party can, after a patent application has been published, submit observations to the Registrar of Patents on the patentability of the invention in the application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The third party provides reasons and documents to the Registrar, which can be useful in the Search and Examination process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This helps to ensure that only deserving inventions are granted patent protection, as the patent examiner has another source of information available to him or her when making that assessment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, third party observations are already being filed, but informally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Setting out the process in legislation makes it clear and transparent for all, and increases awareness about how the process can be used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 11 of the Bill introduces a process for re-examining the specification of a patent after it has been granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After a patent has been granted, information which affects the validity of the patent could come to light, which was not previously available at the earlier stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, a competitor or a researcher could come to know of some document or earlier published literature which may suggest that the invention in question is actually not new or inventive and, therefore, the patent should never have been granted in the first place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the main means of challenging the validity of a patent at the Registry of Patents, after it has been granted, is through the patent revocation process under section 80 of the Patents Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With patent revocation, the requestor is involved as a party in the entire revocation proceeding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This means that all the requestor does is make the request and submit the documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If the patent examiner finds that there are grounds for the patent to be revoked, he will correspond with the patent proprietor only.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Therefore, for the requestor, this provides an additional, lower-cost option to challenge the validity of a patent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This helps to strengthen the quality of granted patents in Singapore, and is the latest step in our efforts to improve the patent system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2013, IPOS began to examine patent applications inhouse, having built up a team of examiners to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our patent examination capabilities were recognised internationally when, in 2014, IPOS was appointed an International Searching and Preliminary Examining Authority for international PCT patent applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2014, we also tightened the system such that a patent is granted only if the invention fully meets the patentability requirements in our law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Now, these latest measures provide even more avenues for third parties to scrutinise and submit information for IPOS to consider, thus helping to further enhance the quality of the Patents Register.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore offers a suite of dispute resolution options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Besides going to the Courts or to IPOS, parties can also consider resolving their disputes by way of arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, arbitration proceedings can take place in private, and parties have a greater degree of control over how the proceedings are conducted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore is also highly-regarded internationally as an arbitration venue, and offers a choice of leading arbitral institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: According to the 2018 International Arbitration Survey by Queen Mary University of London and White & Case, Singapore is now the third most preferred seat of arbitration globally, and the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) the third most preferred arbitral institution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments also clarify that such arbitral awards bind only the parties to the arbitration proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments will provide greater clarity and certainty to users, as well as encourage the use of arbitration in IP disputes, and strengthen Singapore's attractiveness as a venue for international IP arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Arbitral awards cannot affect the status of IP rights on the IP Registers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The arbitral award only affects the parties that have submitted the dispute to arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As Members know, arbitration is essentially an agreement by which two parties agree to submit a dispute to a chosen tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, for example, if an arbitral tribunal finds that a patent issued by any country is invalid, the consequences of such a finding, which, for example, could affect the licence fee payable by one party to the other, affects the parties in the arbitration only, and no one else.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The patent remains on the Register in whichever country it may originate from.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Decisions that affect the status of IP rights on the Registers can only be made by the Courts or the relevant Registrars from the jurisdictions that issue those IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments will lend further certainty to arbitrators and stakeholders who may wish to challenge the validity of IP rights in arbitration proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I turn now to other ancillary amendments related to IP dispute resolution, and I will highlight two main ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This could, for example, lead to cost savings by reducing one layer of appeal, when it is clear that the parties to the dispute before the Registrar of Patents intend to appeal against the Registrar's decision anyway.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, clauses 5, 26, 29 and 33 of the Bill harmonise across all the Acts relating to IP rights the availability of the right to appeal against High Court decisions made on appeal from the relevant Registrar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are giving IP rights owners greater confidence that they can effectively enforce their IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This preserves their incentives to continue investing in innovative and creative activities, which, in turn, benefits our economy and our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These reforms also build on Singapore's considerable strengths, to enhance our standing as a hub for international IP arbitration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By monetising intangible innovations, there is incentive to work on ideas and make them reality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The substantive law governing and protecting IP is a key ingredient in ensuring Singapore's reputation as an IP hub grows.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill strengthens that framework so that IP rights can be better protected in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I go further, Sir, I should declare that I am a practising lawyer whose practice also includes IP and acted in the case that appeared in the Explanatory Statement of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will allow the patent granted to more accurately reflect the scope that would be adequate both for the rights of the proprietor as well as other innovators in the same field.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how this process may affect the turnover time for patent registration in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The re-examination after grant process is found in clause 11, new section 38A of the Patents Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although the applicant has less control in the ex parte proceeding, the applicant does not need to spend as much financial resources and time to challenge the patent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as it is good to provide this alternative process of challenging a patent, would the Minister elaborate on the safeguards to prevent a proprietor of a legitimate patent from getting deluged by these applications?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although the applications may not cost as much for the applicant as a Court proceeding, these applications take a toll on the proprietor by increasing uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One or both of these kinds of third-party processes are present in other jurisdictions and regions, such as Japan, Great Britain, Europe, Australia and China.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having it in Singapore will further our position as an IP hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These processes make patents in Singapore more robust and accurate as there are more avenues to subject them to scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because it is ex parte, these processes are less costly and less time consuming.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is especially important for SMEs with limited resources and manpower, which is a point the Senior Minister of State alluded to in his speech earlier on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to the re-examination after grant process, there is a bar in the new section 38A(5) of the Patents Act against the filing of an application where there is a pending Court proceeding in which the validity of the patent may be put in issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister explain why there is no similar bar in the context of an ongoing arbitration, especially if a party to the arbitration is trying to get a second bite at the cherry by filing an application?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though arbitration proceedings are private, the proprietary holder could, possibly, apply for a stay of the re-examination application.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, certain IP disputes may be carried out at IPOS or at the various levels of Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, copyright proceedings used to be held in "a Court" but has been changed in clauses 3 and 4 to only the High Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The jurisdiction of the Registrar at IPOS to determine infringement of a patent is removed by clause 13.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, this Bill consolidates IP proceedings in the High Court, simplifying and streamlining the process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As cross-border IP disputes may become increasingly common in an interconnected world, overseas enforcement is particularly important for IP disputes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, along with this change comes concerns regarding costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Small businesses already tend to avoid enforcing IP rights due to somewhat prohibitive costs and a potential "war of attrition".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the Bill provides for indemnity costs under certain conditions at clause 6, this is only for Geographical Indications and a trial and hearing at the High Court still costs significantly more than that of a lower Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, as some of the procedures were previously carried out by IPOS, what will be done to ensure that our judiciary has the necessary expertise and resources needed to replace that function?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is important as there is some school of thought that certain IP disputes, such as copyright and registration of trademark or patents, are non-arbitrable as it is against public policy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are some arguments, not necessarily arguments I would agree with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the Review of the Arbitration Act Committee's 2000 Report Review of Arbitration Laws espoused such a view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are advantages to having IP being arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, parties have greater control over where they desire to have a matter arbitrated, for example, in a neutral jurisdiction instead of the place of business.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the new section 52C(3) of the Arbitration Act and 26C(3) of the International Arbitration Act make it clear that an arbitration award involving IP rights does not affect third-party holder of a security interest, could the Minister elaborate on how this will operate?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill sets out exciting changes to the IP dispute resolution landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What will be done to strengthen and train up capabilities of our people so that people in our legal industry can benefit from these changes?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: People who use technology in their day-to-day life will also benefit from this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This also means that if an arbitral tribunal makes a finding that a patent is invalid, a third party will not be able to rely on that finding to argue that he does not infringe the patent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, with the consequent move for IP cases to be heard by the High Court, I am concerned that the costs of arbitration as well as the costs of award will escalate in tandem with IP cases moving to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the formalisation of third party observations on patent applications, when a patent application has been published, but a patent has not been granted, a third party may make submissions to the Registrar of Patents on the patentability of the invention.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Such a formalisation of process is a positive move to ensure the quality of granted patents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With such an exclusive jurisdiction vested in the High Court, I wish to ask the Minister if such a move will overburden the High Court and its judicial officers and overstretch our already lean judiciary.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, will such a move also result in escalation of costs to take action or defend during an IP dispute?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although there is a fast track procedure instituted, will costs be truly and effectively kept down, regardless of the value of disputes or cost-sensitive litigants?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, in our journey towards strengthening our IP regime, encouraging inventions and innovation, can we also do more to help our SMEs, startups, including fintech startups, entrepreneurs and freelance professionals in various sectors, such as those in the creative sector, gaming or software development areas, to help them navigate this area of law and the new disputes regime easily, effectively and in an economical manner as and when they are registering, arbitrating, accused of infringement or taking civil action themselves in the area of IP law which encompasses, trademarks, patents and copyright?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill addresses three broad areas of IP dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have clarifications and recommendations for each of these three areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to commend MinLaw for the extensive public consultation process and outreach to stakeholder groups, such as IPSA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This move, which assists IPOS in evaluating patents at the pre-grants stage, will increase the overall quality of registered patents in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, will the Ministry consider allowing third-party observers the option of remaining anonymous and not revealing their identities to the patent applicant and the general public?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would encourage more third parties to submit observations without any fear of prejudice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Japan Patent Office and the European Patent Office both permit third-party observations to be filed anonymously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To address the concern of frivolous observations being anonymously filed, the identity of third-party observers can be known by only IPOS who can take action against parties who abuse the observation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, will the Ministry consider making the content of third-party observations and the applicant's response to the third-party observation available for public inspection?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Public inspection could generate healthy debate on the validity of the specific patent, making the grant process more robust.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On a broader level, this could increase awareness of the requirements of patent validity as a whole.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would increase the overall quality of registered patents in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the International Patent System administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, observations and the applicant's responses are made available for public inspection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, will the Ministry consider setting out in subsidiary legislation or guidelines the grounds on which pre-grant third-party observations should be based?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the new section 32 on pre-grant observations states that third parties are to provide “reasons” for their observations, it does not define the term “reasons”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In contrast, the new section 38A on the post-grant process explicitly provides grounds for third parties to request a re-examination of patents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Setting out a list of possible “reasons” would increase the clarity of third-party submissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Japan’s Patent Law prescribes specific grounds for third-party observations at the pre-grant stage, which are similar to the grounds under which patents can be invalidated post-grant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Likewise, the European Patent Convention specifies that pre-grant third-party observations on patentability must be based on the grounds of novelty, inventive step, clarity, sufficiency of disclosure and amendments that are not allowed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, while I understand that the costs for third party observations have not been determined and that accessibility would be the key concern, will the Ministry provide its assurance that costs for doing so will be kept as low as possible?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the costs could be a nominal administration fee for the processing of their observations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Keeping the costs low will ensure that third parties keen to submit useful observations are not deterred by the prohibitive costs of doing so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I have two points to raise on the amendments to clarify that IP disputes can be arbitrated in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My two points relate to the scope of IP disputes that can be arbitrated in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can the Minister clarify if IP rights found in employment contracts are arbitrable?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is common practice for employers to insert clauses relating to IP rights in employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are some countries that deem employment disputes to be non-arbitrable because they relate to matters of public policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Greece is one such country that considers employment disputes to be non-arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The position in Singapore on arbitrability of employment disputes has not been conclusively settled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If employment disputes are non-arbitrable, then IP disputes arising from employment contracts may be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Courts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be useful for the Ministry to clarify the position on arbitrability of IP disputes arising out of employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can the Minister clarify if the arbitral awards for patent validity disputes can serve as a basis for patent registry amendments?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Internationally, countries have taken different positions on this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the European Union, patent infringement issues are arbitrable but patent validity challenges are within the exclusive jurisdiction of State Courts and are not arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the other end of the spectrum, Switzerland allows arbitral awards to constitute the basis for amendments to its patent registry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 52F seems to suggest that patent validity is arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it would be useful for the Minister to further clarify whether it is intended that such arbitration award would only be valid as between parties or whether the award can serve as a basis for patent registry amendment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that details of this fast-track option is still being ironed out and will be fleshed out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the proposed cap of two hearing days was derived?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the powers of the trial judge hearing cases on the fast track to order relief.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This question was also left open in the Final Report of the IP Dispute Resolution Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a crucial point that I hope the Ministry will eventually clarify.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to highlight that if fast track judges are unable to make decisions on relief, they may have to pass the case to default track judges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This might lead to more time spent and increased costs if plaintiffs have to bring separate legal proceedings by the plaintiff to obtain the legal remedies sought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their activism and their interest in legal development in their chosen area is something to be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have raised points for clarification in four main areas, and I propose to deal with them as a whole under these four areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether the “specialised track” would be effective in keeping litigation costs down.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked a few questions about the features of the “specialised track”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, Mr Louis Ng's suggestions and proposals in relation to how we design this track, what we take into account, we will consider them when we prepare the relevant rules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The “specialised track” focuses on lowering costs by having simplified processes and other cost-saving features.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These obviously have to deal with the appropriate types of cases and not every case will be suitable for this "specialised" track.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will elaborate on some of the features which we are considering although they are not part of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There will be early and active case management by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will ensure that cases are managed in an appropriate manner, with procedures that are streamlined and cost-effective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we sieve the cases upfront to ensure that they are appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The “specialised track” is appropriate for lower-value cases, which tend to be less complex.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The cap on the value of the claim reflects this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will also help to lower the business risk of litigation that Members spoke about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, if a case is being heard and halfway through, you might need another half a day, obviously the trial judge will have the discretion to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will reduce the time spent and, consequently, the costs for the parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The cap on two days, Mr Louis Ng asked how it was arrived at.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was based on the recommendations of the IP Resolution Review Committee which, I am sure, Mr Louis Ng knows comprises representatives from the judiciary as well as IP lawyers who handle these cases, academia and also IP-rich companies which viewed this as appropriate for the less complex cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we took a sampling of these views and proposed the two days on that basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Regarding the relief that the trial judge can grant, it is intended that the trial judge’s power to grant interim and final relief would be the same, whether a case is on the “specialised track” or “default track”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the remedies that one would expect to see ought not be different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is just that the process and the speed by which you resolve the case could be different, depending on the complexity and nature of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Regarding appeals, final decisions in cases on the “specialised track” will be appealable in the same manner as final decisions in cases on the “default track”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the appeal is a separate process, the time spent on the appeal hearing is not included in the two-day hearing cap for cases on the “specialised track”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether the costs of arbitration of IP disputes will escalate as a result of moving certain IP disputes to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Also, when we look at the feedback from the Committee, that is also not the sense that they got.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we will continue to monitor this as we actually implement this process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, parties choose arbitration sometimes for different reasons from why they have the matter resolved in Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the expertise and resources required by the High Court, pursuant to the consolidation of civil IP disputes in the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned in my speech earlier, the High Court already has a specialist bench of IP judges, with greater expertise and experience in IP matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My Ministry will continue to work with the Courts to ensure that there are sufficient resources to handle the caseload as may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I next turn to Mr Louis Ng and Mr Christopher de Souza’s questions around the rigour of the third-party observation process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will just address queries that have been raised together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, as far as anonymity is concerned – I think Mr Louis Ng raised this point – if there is no identifier on the documents containing the third-party observation, then the identity of the third-party observer will not be known.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in other words, you can choose to be anonymous or not anonymous as you wish as a third party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Louis Ng also asked about whether the records will be available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The records of the patent search and examination history are available to the public on the Patents Open Dossier service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will include the contents of the third-party observations filed before the deadline as well as the applicant’s response to the examiner’s written opinion incorporating any observation, where there is one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all of that will be made available on the Patents Open Dossier service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I touched on this in my earlier speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The statutory requirements for an invention to be patentable can be found in section 13 of the Patents Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, for example, the third party could make an observation that an invention is not new because of an earlier publication.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that helps to address Members' concern about an overall prolongation of the process because of the observations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A healthy patent regime encourages innovation and protects only deserving inventions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third-party observations which are meritorious contribute to this and would be worth the time taken to consider it, so that, overall, we develop a more robust and a more trustworthy IP system and regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked a few questions about the post-grant patent re-examination process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When a re-examination request is made, the specification of the patent will first be re-examined by a patent Examiner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Examiner would ask the patent proprietor to respond only if there are possible grounds for the patent to be revoked.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This avoids placing an unnecessary burden on the patent proprietor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Christopher de Souza asked why there is no bar against filing a re-examination request when there is an ongoing arbitration proceeding in which the validity of the patent may be put in issue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is because arbitration proceedings cannot affect the status of the patent on the Patents Register.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast, proceedings before the Court or IPOS in which the validity of the patent may be an issue could lead to the patent being revoked.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the patent itself being revoked as opposed to the right between two parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, the new section 38A(5) is necessary to prevent concurrent proceedings in which the status of the patent on the Patents Register could be affected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is not applicable in the context of arbitration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Christopher de Souza asked some questions about the arbitrability of IP disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, as to whether IP rights found in employment contracts are arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill is intended to clarify that a wide range of IP disputes are arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In employment contracts, it is common to find clauses about the ownership of IP rights that arise in the employee’s course of work, and I think that is what Mr Louis Ng seemed to be referring to in his speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there are disputes subsequently about the ownership of these IP rights, then these disputes are arbitrable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to add that what is arbitrable does not necessarily mean that it will be the subject of an arbitration because it is still defined by the scope of the arbitration agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Louis Ng asked whether the arbitral awards for patent validity disputes can serve as a basis to amend the patent on the Register.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my speech earlier, I had explained that the arbitral awards only affect the parties to the arbitration agreement and will not affect the status of IP rights on the Registers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is because we take the view that decisions that affect the status of IP rights on the Registers should only be made by the Courts or the relevant Registrars from the jurisdictions that issued those IP rights, since these are decisions that affect the world at large concerning the registration and not just the parties to the arbitration proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is true not only of patents, but of other forms of registrable IP rights, such as trademarks and also registered designs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how an arbitration award involving IP rights affects a third-party holder of a security interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such an award does not affect any existing right or liability between a third-party holder of a security interest and a party to the arbitral proceedings, whether arising in contract or arising by operation of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this is clarified in the new section 52C(3) of the Arbitration Act and section 26C(3) of the International Arbitration Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to the other queries that had been raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked whether more could be done to help SMEs and startups navigate the IP registration and dispute resolution regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The IPOS website provides useful information on the IP registration system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If anyone requires further assistance, they can always call IPOS for help with queries or make an appointment to see an officer at IPOS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For assistance with IP-related disputes, there are legal clinics at IPOS, where there is a panel of lawyers available to provide preliminary advice on, for example, infringement or opposition matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: IPOS also runs complimentary IP business clinics that allow participants to speak with private business consultants on IP strategies, franchising and licensing, audits and valuation, among other issues related to or arising from IP rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the efforts to strengthen our legal industry, so that they can benefit from these reforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My Ministry and the relevant agencies will be engaging stakeholders in the IP and legal sector to explain how these changes can benefit them, how they will operate in this new landscape, and how they could make use of it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will not just extend to practitioners, but also businesses in the business environment, big and small companies which use the system, and whom our IP regime is really intended to support, in other words, the stakeholders who benefit from the IP regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Christopher de Souza also raised a point about costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point that Mr Christopher de Souza made was why is it that the Bill provides for indemnity cost under certain conditions in clause 6, but only for geographical indications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wish to thank the Members who have spoken and who have supported the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.57 pm until 4.20 pm.
